01.event: Rabbi Elazar taught that the unlearned will not be resurrected, and his teacher Rabbi Yohanan objected that God is not pleased by such a statement.
01.turn: Seeing Rabbi Yohanan grieved, Rabbi Elazar searched for and found a remedy for the unlearned.
01.outcome: He taught that one who marries his daughter to a scholar or supports scholars is credited as cleaving to the Divine Presence, and so merits life.
01.summary: Rabbi Elazar taught that ordinary uneducated people would not rise at the resurrection. His teacher Rabbi Yohanan protested that God would not be pleased to hear this said of them, and Rabbi Elazar defended it from another verse. But seeing how distressed Rabbi Yohanan was, Rabbi Elazar told him he had found a remedy: whoever marries his daughter to a scholar, or does business for scholars, or benefits them from his property, is considered as cleaving to God and so lives.

02.event: The priestly court set widows' marriage contracts at one hundred dinars, then raised them to two hundred when widows were demeaned.
02.turn: Grooms then stopped marrying priestly widows in favor of Israelite virgins at the same price.
02.outcome: The court restored the original amount.
02.summary: The priestly court originally fixed a marriage contract of 400 dinars for a virgin and 100 for a widow. When they saw widows being treated with contempt they raised the widow's sum to 200, but then men avoided priestly widows, preferring to marry an Israelite virgin for the same price, so the court restored the old amounts. It is an institutional history rather than a story about particular people.

03.actor: Rav Aha son of Rav Avya
03.event: Rav Aha met Rav Ashi's students and asked whether their master had said anything about the doorway-form.
03.outcome: They told him Rav Ashi had said nothing.
03.summary: Rav Aha, son of Rav Avya, came upon Rav Ashi's students and asked whether Rav Ashi had taught anything about the form of a doorway. They answered that he had said nothing at all.
03.missing: Any consequence of the exchange; it is a brief encounter serving a legal point.

04.event: A case arose in Rav Hisda's study hall, which Rav Hisda brought to Rav Huna's study hall.
04.outcome: They resolved it from a mishna about an agent and consecrated property.
04.summary: An actual case came up in Rav Hisda's study hall; he brought it to Rav Huna's, and there they settled it by citing a mishna about an owner who tells his agent to fetch an item. The case itself is only gestured at; the rest is legal reasoning.
04.missing: The facts of the incident itself are not described.

05.event: Rabban Gamliel's daughter was married to his brother Abba.
05.outcome: Rabban Gamliel took his brother's other wife, his daughter's rival wife, in levirate marriage.
05.summary: Rabban Gamliel's daughter was married to his brother Abba, who also had another wife. Abba died without children, and Rabban Gamliel performed levirate marriage with the other wife, his daughter's co-wife. The Gemara then debates what this case proves.

07.event: A woman named Me'oret made her slave perform three of the dangerous actions in sequence.
07.summary: A woman named Me'oret made her slave do three of the six dangerous acts, such as travel, bloodletting and bathing, and he died. The Gemara cites it only to argue about whether doing them out of order is fatal.
07.missing: Why she did it and any details of the episode.

08.event: Rabbi Yosei met Elijah the prophet and asked him how a wife helps her husband.
08.outcome: Elijah answered that she turns his raw wheat and flax into bread and clothing, lighting his eyes and standing him on his feet.
08.summary: Rabbi Yosei encountered Elijah the prophet and asked him what the verse means when it calls a wife a helper. Elijah replied that a man brings home raw wheat and flax, which he cannot eat or wear as they are; his wife transforms them, and so she brightens his eyes and sets him on his feet.

09.actor: Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda and Rabba
09.event: A bill of divorce dated by the governor of Bascar came up, and Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda sent the question to Rabba.
09.outcome: Rabba replied that even Rabbi Meir would accept it, since the governor belongs to the kingdom.
09.summary: A divorce document turned up dated by the years of the governor of Bascar rather than the king. Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda sent the question to Rabba, who ruled that it was valid even by Rabbi Meir's strict view, because the governor is an official of that same kingdom.

10.event: A dying Madonite wished to give away his many movable goods as gifts.
10.turn: The Sages told him the only way was to transfer them by means of land, so he bought a small rocky plot near Jerusalem.
10.outcome: He assigned the land with the sheep and barrels to a recipient, died, and the Sages carried out his wishes.
10.summary: A man from Madon living in Jerusalem had a great deal of movable property and, when ill, wanted to give it away. The Sages told him the only remedy was to transfer it along with land, so he bought a rocky plot near Jerusalem and declared that its northern part, with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels, went to a certain person. He died, and the Sages upheld his gift.

11.actor: Rava and Rav Mari bar Rahel
11.event: Rava declared Rav Mari bar Rahel, son of a gentile father and Jewish mother, fit to marry into Israel.
11.outcome: Rava appointed him one of the officials of Babylonia.
11.summary: Rav Mari bar Rahel was the son of a gentile father and a Jewish mother. Rava ruled that his lineage was unflawed and even appointed him an official in Babylonia, reasoning that because his mother was Jewish he counted as one 'from among your brethren'.

12.event: When the exiles returned from Babylonia they camped by a particular well.
12.outcome: The prophets among them permitted drawing from it on a Festival, following an ancestral custom.
12.summary: When the exiles came back from Babylonia they camped beside one particular well, and the prophets among them allowed them to draw water from it on a Festival. The Gemara adds that this was really an inherited custom that the prophets let them continue.
12.missing: Little actual event beyond the encampment; it explains a custom.

13.event: Rava publicly taught that one may scatter straw on a muddy courtyard on Shabbat in the ordinary way.
13.turn: Rav Pappa challenged him with a baraita requiring an unusual manner.
13.outcome: Rava appointed a speaker and publicly announced that his teaching had been a mistake.
13.summary: Rava taught that a courtyard turned muddy by rain on Shabbat may be covered with straw. Rav Pappa objected with a baraita saying the straw may only be scattered with the bottom of a broken basket. Rava then set up a public speaker and announced that what he had said was his own mistake, restating the correct rule in Rabbi Eliezer's name.

14.event: In high spirits Abaye declared himself ready like ben Azzai to answer any question.
14.turn: One of the Sages challenged him on why he read the slave-redemption verses leniently.
14.outcome: Abaye answered that the Torah is lenient toward the Hebrew slave; the debate continues.
14.summary: Abaye once boasted that he was like ben Azzai in the markets of Tiberias, ready to answer anything. A scholar promptly tested him: why interpret the verses on redeeming a Hebrew slave leniently rather than stringently? Abaye replied that the Torah shows concern for the slave's welfare, and the exchange turns into an extended legal argument with no clear end.
14.missing: The end of the exchange; it continues as legal discussion past the passage.

15.event: Visiting Neharde'a, Rav Avya saw a man tying a door bolt with a reed.
15.outcome: He ruled that this door may not be locked with that bolt on Shabbat.
15.summary: When Rav Avya came to Neharde'a he saw a man fastening a bolt to a door with a reed. He declared that the door could not be locked with it on Shabbat, since the bolt was not properly attached.

16.event: In a shepherds' village an inlet of the sea broke through a courtyard wall.
16.outcome: The case came before Rav Yehuda, who required only a single board to permit carrying.
16.summary: Rav Yosef recalled an incident in a shepherds' village where a narrow inlet of the sea had breached an entire wall of a courtyard. The case was brought to Rav Yehuda, who ruled that one upright board was enough to keep the courtyard permitted.

17.event: Abaye posed a difficulty to Rav Dimi about Rabbi Yohanan's view, and Rav Dimi fell silent.
17.outcome: Rav Dimi praised him, saying it was as if Abaye had been present when Rabbi Yohanan taught it.
17.summary: Abaye challenged Rav Dimi with a contradiction in Rabbi Yohanan's rulings, and Rav Dimi had no answer. Abaye then suggested the resolution himself: the Egyptian convert's case depends on a verse that ties status to birth. Rav Dimi exclaimed that he had seen Abaye's head among the pillars when Rabbi Yohanan taught this, praising him as though he had been there.

18.event: Throughout Rav Huna's lifetime Rav Hisda was asked even about cooking an egg in a dairy dish.
18.outcome: He refused to rule, out of deference to his teacher.
18.summary: As long as his teacher Rav Huna was alive, Rav Hisda declined to issue rulings, even on a question as simple as cooking an egg in a dairy dish. It is cited as a pattern of conduct rather than a single episode.
18.missing: A single concrete occasion; it describes ongoing behavior.

19.event: The Sages urged Rabbi Abba bar Zavda to marry and have children.
19.turn: He replied that if he deserved children he would have had them from his first wife, but the real reason was revealed: he had become impotent from Rav Huna's long lectures.
19.outcome: He put the Sages off with an excuse and did not remarry.
19.summary: The Sages told Rabbi Abba bar Zavda to take a wife and have children. He answered that had he been worthy he would already have had children from his first wife. The Gemara explains that this was only an excuse: he had in fact become impotent from holding himself back during Rav Huna's lengthy discourses.

20.event: Nearly blind in old age, Rav Yehuda struggled to read documents before signing them.
20.turn: Ulla told him it was unnecessary, since great authorities had scribes read documents to them.
20.summary: Rav Yehuda, whose sight was failing, went to great effort to read documents himself before signing them. Ulla told him he need not, because Rabbi Elazar in the Land of Israel and Rav Nahman had court scribes read documents aloud to them before they signed. The Gemara adds limits on when this is allowed.
20.missing: Whether Rav Yehuda followed the advice.
